newsitem.title: USA: US consumer spending seen simmering down - Blinder.
newsitem.headline: US consumer spending seen simmering down - Blinder.

text.p: U.S. inflation remains benign and two consecutive months of weak retail sales data suggest consumer spending is probably calming down, said Alan Blinder, a former Federal Reserve vice-chairman.
"With two weak retail sales numbers in a row now, it does appear, and I stick my verb advisedly, appear that the consumer is simmering down," Blinder told Reuters in an interview.
Blinder said a cooling off of consumer spending from the rip-roaring rates seen in last quarter of last year and the first quarter of 1997 "would be welcome" for two main reasons.
"First the economy has been growing at an unsustainably rapid rate and second Americans don't save enough," he said.

The Commerce Department released its retail sales report earlier this week, which showed sales dropped 0.3 percent in April. The March data was revised downward to unchanged from a previously reported 0.1 percent rise.
Excluding autos, retail sales fell 0.1 percent in April.
The ex-Fed chairman said inflation numbers remained subdued while real growth rate in the economy continued to be strong although with some signs of slowing.
"The inflation numbers continue to be benign, (but) it's not astonishing.
"And the real growth numbers have been extremely buoyant of late, although with some signs of a slowdown. So that's about the best combination you can possibly hope for," Blinder said.

The Labor Department announced on Wedensday a surprising 0.6 percent drop in the Producer Price Index (PPI) for April, the biggest drop since August 1993. The core rate, which excludes energy and food prices, dropped 0.1 percent.
The overall March PPI was down 0.1 percent.
"I think the long and short of it is that the economy is throwing off data that can hardly be better, and the question, of course, in everybody's mind is, Will it keep up?" he said.
Blinder said he sees no credit crunch in the U.S., saying that he thinks there is "plenty of credit, and (there) has been for some time."
The former Fed official said, however, the price of credit in the country is modestly high.

"The prices of credit are still, relative to inflation, that is in real terms, modestly high, not modestly low. And that's across the whole yield curve, for long-term credit and for short term credit. (But) they're not extraordinarily high, we've seen them a lot higher than this.
"But I don't think it's possible to look at real interest rates these days in the United States, given a 2.5 percent inflation, and say they're exceptionally low," Blinder said.
The former Fed vice-chairman said U.S. labor markets are currently tight and are likely to remain so in the near future.
"The labor market has been tight for some time and it's likely to continue tight for some time.
"The big question on a lot of people's minds is whether that stunning 4.9 (percent unemployment) number we got in the last unemployment report (April) will persist," he said.
Blinder also said he believes inventories are currently being re-built after strong sales earlier in the year.
"I think inventories are being replaced now. You had a little upcreep in inventories, (and) you had a considerable inventory accumulation in the first quarter," he said.
Blinder said he did not want to comment or forecast the outcome of the next meeting of the Fed's policy-setting body on May 20.
The economist left the Fed in January 1996. He currently holds the chair of economics at Princeton Univeristy.

Blinder also said the current economic cycle is different from 1994. He said that when the Fed began its tightening cycle then, the so-called "real" federal funds rate, or federal funds rate minus the annual rate of retail inflation, stood close to zero.
"That's an extraordinarily easy monetary policy. And it was very clear to everybody (at the time) that the Fed funds rate would have to go up by a substantial amount," he said.
He said, however, that "this time around, when you start around with (real) fed funds around 2-3/4 percent, you're starting from a fundamentally different position."
